evidence_quotes.quote: Using a cross-case qualitative methodology, we illustrate how power and control translate into practices, leading to different levels of local government involvement in service delivery.
Six District Councils where these four development partners operate were also included in the study.
Rules and accountability requirements, typically with regard to the handling of project funds, also governed the partnerships between local governments and their development partners.

Further research could investigate which levels of local government involvement in service delivery (leading, partaking or supervising) provide the best outcomes, in terms of value for money, sustainability or citizen participation for example.

criterion_notes.c1: Although the empirical setting is organisations drilling boreholes in Malawi's rural water supply sector, the study does not examine household or community water service access; it investigates inter-organisational collaboration between District Councils and development partners.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording of Criterion 2: YES — the study examines institutional, administrative, and governance factors in decentralised rural service delivery, including District Council mandates under the Local Government Act of 1998, inter-organisational power relations, and bureaucratic financial accountability rules between local governments and donors/NGOs. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the factors studied concern inter-organisational project delivery, planning coordination, and donor grant disbursement between NGOs/donors and District Councils rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure requirements, tariffs or cost-recovery rules, disconnection/enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing consumer access). Note: even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the study fails Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 (no water service access outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative cross-case study drawing on an 8-month onsite ethnography (June–December 2011) of planning meetings and recorded, transcribed interviews with key representatives across four development organisations and six District Councils in Malawi.
criterion_notes.c4: No household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is measured or reported. The sole outcome analysed is the organisational level of local government involvement in cross-sector partnerships (little to no involvement, coordinating, partaking, or leading service delivery), and the authors explicitly note in the conclusion that service outcomes are left for future research.
criterion_notes.c5: The organisational sample and unit of analysis (cross-sector partnerships across 4 development partners and 6 District Councils), explanatory constructs (inter-organisational power and control mechanisms), organisational outcome (level of local government involvement), and qualitative cross-case study design are clearly reported, confirming that the outcome and exposure fall outside review scope.

study_design: Qualitative cross-case comparative study (8-month onsite ethnography and semi-structured interviews)
population_and_sample: Cross-sector partnerships between four development organisations in the rural water supply sector (Unicef, HydroConsult, WaterAid, Concern Universal) and six District Councils in Malawi (unit of analysis: inter-organisational partnership; 8-month ethnography plus 2 to 4 formal interviews per organisation)
exposure: Inter-organisational power practices (discursive legitimacy in planning, formal authority in project mandates and supervision, command over donor project funds) and Ouchi control mechanisms (clan-based trust, market-based interest alignment, bureaucratic financial accountability rules)
outcome: Level of local government involvement in cross-sector service delivery partnerships (little to no involvement, coordinating service delivery, partaking in service delivery, or leading service delivery)
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 and Criterion 1). Although situated in Malawi's rural water supply sector, this qualitative cross-case study examines how inter-organisational power and control shape cross-sector partnerships between donors/NGOs and District Councils. Its outcome is strictly organisational—the level of local government involvement in project delivery (little to no involvement, coordinating, partaking, or leading)—with no empirical measurement of household or community water access, availability, reliability, affordability, or exclusion (explicitly deferred to future research on p. 204 / PDF p. 13). In addition, under the 2026-10-13 narrow Criterion 2 reading, the donor-council project planning and fund-disbursement practices examined are inter-organisational project delivery governance rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access.
